opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the key change with the reasoning models, starting with o1, is that we found a new dimension to scale. Before that, scaling laws mostly meant pre-training: more parameters, more data, more compute, and the loss goes down quite predictably. That curve hasn't stopped, but it's getting more expensive, and high-quality data is starting to become a real bottleneck.

What o1 showed is that you can also scale the thinking itself. You can scale reinforcement learning compute during training, and you can scale inference compute at test time, letting the model think longer. Both give fairly clean improvements, especially on tasks with verifiable answers like math, competitive programming, and some science problems. For someone like me who has worked on reinforcement learning for a long time, that's very exciting, because for years RL was seen as unstable, and now it's becoming a scalable recipe on top of a strong pre-trained model.

That said, I'd be careful about calling it a solved scaling law. A few things are still open.

First, it works best where the reward is clear. When you can check whether the answer is right, RL scales nicely. For open-ended tasks like writing, research judgment, or long agentic tasks in the real world, the reward is fuzzy, and scaling is much harder. I think a lot of the next progress will come from that: better reward models, better environments, and better ways of getting feedback.

Second, longer thinking is not automatically better thinking. Models sometimes overthink, go around in circles, or burn tokens on easy questions. So efficiency, knowing when to think hard and when to just answer, is an important research problem in its own right, not just an engineering detail.

Third, the biggest frontier, in my view, is agents: models that act over many steps, use tools, interact with environments, and recover from mistakes. Reasoning is the foundation for that, but going from solving a math problem in one long chain of thought to finishing a real task over hours or days needs new infrastructure, especially large-scale RL systems and environments. That's a big part of why I care so much about RL infrastructure.

So overall I'm quite optimistic. The reasoning paradigm opened a second scaling curve, and we're still fairly early on it. But the easy part, verifiable tasks with clean rewards, is moving fastest. The harder and more interesting part is extending this to the messy, open-ended tasks where most real value lies.

r001.rationale: The response discusses scaling and the o1 reasoning paradigm but does not say OpenAI has more capable models internally than it has released publicly.

r002.rationale: The response says it is optimistic, describes reasoning as a second scaling curve that is still early, and explains that scaling training and inference compute improves performance.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing to say is that the scaling law itself hasn't broken, but the axis along which we're scaling has changed. For a long time, scaling meant pretraining: more parameters, more data, more compute, and you got a fairly predictable drop in loss. What the o-series showed is that there's a second axis, which is reinforcement learning on reasoning, and a third axis, which is test-time compute. Those two are coupled. You train the model to think longer and more carefully, and then at inference you let it actually use that budget.

From my perspective, coming from reinforcement learning, the interesting part is that the RL scaling curve looks surprisingly clean when the reward is verifiable. Math, code, anything where you can check the answer, the model improves in a way that tracks compute quite well. That's why the jumps from o1 to o3 on benchmarks like AIME or competition programming felt so steep. It wasn't a new architecture, it was that the RL loop finally had enough signal and enough scale.

Where I'm more cautious is in generalization. The question everyone should be asking is whether the reasoning ability learned on verifiable domains transfers to tasks where there's no clean reward, like open-ended research, long-horizon agent work, or judgment calls with ambiguous criteria. My honest read is that it transfers partially. You see better planning and self-correction in general, but the gap between "solved a hard math problem" and "reliably completed a week-long engineering task" is still large. Closing that gap is less about raw scaling and more about building environments and reward signals that reflect what we actually care about.

So if you ask me to judge the progress, I'd say the reasoning paradigm has given us at least one more full cycle of predictable improvement, and that's a big deal. But I'd separate two claims. The claim that reasoning models keep getting better with more RL compute, I believe. The claim that this alone takes us to general intelligence without solving the reward and environment problem, I'm not yet convinced of. The next year or two will tell us a lot, mainly through how well these models perform as agents rather than as test-takers.

astra-6.text:
I would separate two questions: are the models getting better, and do we understand the law governing that improvement? Those are related, but they’re not the same.

With reasoning models, the interesting idea is that you can spend computation not only during training, but also while solving a problem. Instead of producing an answer immediately, the model can explore possibilities, check intermediate steps, and revise its approach. That gives us another dimension along which capability might scale.

But more computation doesn’t automatically mean better reasoning. If a model follows the wrong direction, thinking longer may just extend the mistake. The important question is whether it can use that additional computation productively—and whether the improvement holds on unfamiliar problems where checking the answer is difficult.

So I would judge progress by the relationship between compute, reliability, and generalization. How much additional computation does a meaningful improvement require? Does it help across different kinds of tasks? And does it reduce fundamental errors, rather than simply improve a benchmark score? I’d be optimistic about the direction, but cautious about treating evidence of improvement as a complete scaling law for intelligence.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to distinguish between scaling training and scaling the computation used to answer a question. For reasoning models, the interesting possibility is that giving a model more time to work through a problem can improve its answer. That gives us another dimension along which to scale.

But I would be careful about equating better benchmark results with a general scaling law for intelligence. We need to ask: How consistently does extra computation help? Does it help on unfamiliar problems? And what does that improvement cost?

So I see reasoning models as a promising direction, but I wouldn’t claim that the long-term trajectory is settled. The stronger evidence would be reliable improvements across a broad range of tasks, especially tasks where checking the answer is difficult.
